summary: The Seunas, or Yadavas of Devagiri, were Chalukya feudatories until Bhillama V seized Kalyani around 1187, declared himself king and built the hill fortress of Devagiri. Under Simhana II (c. 1200/1210–1246) they ruled the western Deccan from the Narmada to the Tungabhadra, and Marathi became a language of government and literature under their rule. Alauddin Khalji's raid of 1296 made them tributaries of Delhi, Malik Kafur took Devagiri in 1307–08 and again in 1313, and the kingdom was annexed in 1317.

details: Bhillama V became Yadava ruler around 1175, while his nominal overlords, the Chalukyas of Kalyani, were collapsing. Around 1187 he took the old Chalukya capital, Kalyani, declared himself a sovereign king and founded a new capital at Devagiri, a formidable natural hill stronghold. But the Hoysala king Veera Ballala II was also claiming the Chalukya lands. In the late 1180s, or around 1191 by another account, Ballala decisively defeated Bhillama's army at Soratur, in present-day Gadag district. The Yadavas were driven north of the Malaprabha and Krishna rivers, which formed their southern border for the next two decades.

Bhillama's son Jaitugi, king from about 1191, turned east against the Kakatiyas of Telangana. The Seuna dynasty article dates his invasion to around 1194. The Kakatiya king Mahadeva was killed in the fighting around 1198-1199, and some historians think his predecessor Rudradeva had also died fighting Jaitugi. Mahadeva's son Ganapati was taken captive and later released as a Yadava vassal, marrying Jaitugi's daughter. For years the Kakatiyas accepted Yadava overlordship, giving Devagiri influence over much of the eastern Deccan as well as the west.

Jaitugi's son Simhana II, who came to the throne around 1200 or 1210, is regarded as the dynasty's greatest king. While the Hoysalas were busy in the Tamil south, he pushed across the Malaprabha. Yadava inscriptions appear there from 1202, and by 1213 most of present-day Dharwad district had been annexed. Banavasi fell before 1215, and by 1220 everything north of the Tungabhadra was his. The Rattas of Saundatti, former Hoysala vassals, became his feudatories and helped him expand south. The Yadava kingdom's southern frontier now ran along the Tungabhadra river.

To the north, across the Narmada, lay Malwa, ruled by the Paramara dynasty. In 1215 Simhana invaded it successfully. His court poet Hemadri later claimed that the Paramara king Arjunavarman was killed, but an inscription of 1222 mentions only his defeat, so the claim is doubtful. The raid brought plunder and prestige rather than new land. Malwa stayed Paramara, and the Narmada remained roughly the northern limit of Yadava power. Later Yadava kings defeated the weakening Paramaras again before 1250 and in the 1270s, without annexing their land.

The Shilaharas of Kolhapur, in the south-west of present-day Maharashtra, had been feudatories but had asserted their independence under King Bhoja II. In 1216 Simhana attacked him, and Bhoja fled to the hill fort of Panhala. The Shilahara territory, including Kolhapur, appears to have been annexed before 1217. Simhana's general Bichana later subdued other restless southern chiefs, among them the Guttas of Dharwad and the Kadambas of Hangal and Goa. At its height Simhana's kingdom probably stretched from the Narmada to the Tungabhadra and from the Arabian Sea to western Telangana.

Lata, a coastal region of present-day Gujarat, kept shifting its loyalty between the Yadavas, the Paramaras and the Chaulukyas of Gujarat. In 1220 Simhana sent his general Kholeshvara there. Kholeshvara killed the local ruler Simha and captured Lata, and Simhana made Simha's relative Shankha a Yadava vassal. The Chaulukya general Lavanaprasada struck back and took the port of Khambhat, and Shankha's counter-attacks with Yadava help failed. The struggle ended in a peace treaty around 1232. A later Yadava invasion of Gujarat in the 1240s failed, and the general Rama, Kholeshvara's son, was killed.

Simhana's grandson Krishna (c. 1246-1261) fought inconclusive wars with the Paramaras, the Vaghelas of Gujarat and the Hoysalas. His younger brother Mahadeva (c. 1261-1270) saw an opening in the east, where the new Kakatiya queen Rudrama Devi faced rebellions. He invaded Telangana, and Yadava records boast of victories over the ruler of Tilinga. But a Kakatiya inscription says their general Bhairava defeated the Yadava army, probably in or after 1263, and the invasion appears to have been repulsed. Mahadeva's invasion of the Hoysala kingdom was also turned back. The age of easy Yadava expansion was over.

When Mahadeva died around 1270 his son Ammana became king, but after a short reign he was dethroned by his cousin Ramachandra, son of King Krishna. Ramachandra pursued an aggressive policy. In the 1270s he defeated the weakened Paramaras of Malwa, and in 1275 his general Tikkama led a powerful army into the Hoysala kingdom, gathering great plunder before he was forced to retreat in 1276. Ramachandra also pushed the north-eastern frontier, subduing Bhandara and occupying Tripuri, the old Kalachuri capital near Jabalpur. But he lost Raichur and other lands to the Kakatiyas.

The Yadavas were the first major dynasty to use Marathi as an official language, and early Marathi literature emerged under their rule. Hemadri, a minister at the Yadava court, tried to formalise Marathi with Sanskrit expressions to raise its status. Around 1290, during Ramachandra's reign, the saint-poet Dnyaneshwar wrote the Dnyaneshwari, a Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, bringing a sacred Sanskrit text into the everyday language. The Mahanubhava sect also spread Marathi as a literary language. The Yadava age left a lasting cultural mark on the region even as its political power waned.

In 1296 Alauddin Khalji, then governor of Kara for the Delhi Sultanate, led a secret raid across the Vindhyas, spreading word that he was heading for Chanderi. He reached Devagiri while the main Yadava army was away under Ramachandra's son Simhana and the fort was short of supplies. Ramachandra withdrew into the hilltop citadel while the lower city was plundered. When Simhana returned and fought, he was defeated, and the Yadavas agreed to a much larger indemnity and tribute from the Achalpur province. Alauddin used the wealth to seize the Delhi throne, but the tribute went unpaid.

Ramachandra's unpaid tribute kept mounting. In 1307 (some sources say 1308) Alauddin, now sultan, sent his general Malik Kafur with a huge army, helped by the governors of Malwa and Gujarat. They overcame Devagiri's weakened forces almost without a battle, and Ramachandra was taken to Delhi. Alauddin reinstated him as a tributary ruler in return for help against the kingdoms farther south. Devagiri became Delhi's base in the Deccan: in 1310 Kafur marched from there against the Kakatiyas, and in 1311 against the Hoysalas. The Yadava kingdom survived only as a client of Delhi.

Ramachandra died around 1311, and his successor Simhana III, also called Shankaradeva, challenged Delhi's supremacy and refused to keep paying tribute. In 1313 Alauddin sent Malik Kafur back to Devagiri. Simhana III was killed in the fighting, and the Khalji army occupied the city. Kafur stayed on as governor for about two years, turning the Yadava capital into a Delhi province in all but name. A last king, Harapaladeva, held the Yadava title from 1313, but real power in the western Deccan had passed to the sultans of Delhi.

After Alauddin Khalji died and Mubarak Shah took over in Delhi in 1316, the Yadava prince Harapaladeva ruled briefly as the dynasty's last king. In 1317, according to the Seuna dynasty article, the kingdom was annexed outright by the Khalji sultanate, ending some 130 years of Yadava sovereignty (the same article elsewhere gives 1308, when Ramachandra became a vassal). Devagiri became the seat of Delhi's power in the Deccan, and Muhammad bin Tughluq later renamed it Daulatabad. Thirty years later, rebel Delhi officers at Daulatabad founded the Bahmani Sultanate.
